notes.meaning: Asaph, one of King David's chief singers, wrote this song. He cried out loud to God, and he says it twice. That shows how earnest and desperate he was. In his trouble he did not run to people first. He went straight to God and asked to be heard.

When trouble came, he went looking for the Lord. All night he kept his hands stretched out in prayer and did not stop. Yet nothing seemed to comfort him, much like Jacob, who would not be comforted when he thought his son Joseph was dead. Hard days should be days of prayer. Our troubles are to be prayed away, not drunk away or laughed away.

You would expect that thinking about God would bring comfort. Instead it made him groan, because he could only think of God as angry with him. The more he thought, the weaker his spirit felt. "Selah" seems to mark a pause, a moment to stop and let the sadness sink in.

He could not sleep. It felt as if God were holding his eyes open, with his sorrows standing guard like watchmen. He was so upset he could not even find words. Small troubles talk a lot, but great griefs often go silent.

He thought back to the old days, when God did great things for his people. But at first this only made him feel worse. He compared those bright times with his dark present. Looking back can help, but it can also make today seem even harder.

At night he remembered the songs of thanks he used to sing in happier times. Now he could not sing them. So he searched his own heart deeply. He wanted to know why God was dealing with him like this and when his sorrow would end.

Here are his darkest fears, spoken honestly. Has God turned away for good? Is his "loving devotion" (his faithful, never-quitting love) gone? Have his promises failed, or has his anger shut off his kindness like a spring blocked at its mouth? Every one of these questions has the answer "No," and Scripture says so again and again: God's mercy lasts forever, and he cannot lie. Asking the questions out loud starts to expose how foolish the fear really is. The "Selah" is a pause in the struggle.

This is the turning point. The words are hard to translate. Many older Bibles read, "This is my weakness." On that reading, he catches himself and admits that his doubts come from weak faith, not from any change in God. Then he decides to remember the years when God's "right hand," meaning his power, worked for his people. Some older translators put it this way: the right hand of the Most High can change everything.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Several scholars read the line as the Berean Standard Bible (BSB) translation in these notes does. On this reading his real grief is that God's right hand seems to have changed. He is stating his sorrow plainly, not correcting himself yet.

notes.meaning: Now he makes a firm choice. He will remember what the Lord has done, especially his wonders long ago. The word can also mean to tell about them and praise them out loud. Memory becomes faith's helper. Like Joseph opening the storehouses during the famine, memory brings out stored-up reasons to trust God.

He will think long and carefully about all God has done. That is more than a quick glance. He will let God's works soak into his mind, and that kind of deep thinking leads to good talk. Talking about God's deeds helps both the speaker and the people who hear.

God's way is holy. Even when we cannot understand what he is doing, we can be sure that everything he does is pure, right and good. Older Bibles read "in the sanctuary," the place of worship, where God makes his ways known to his people. No so-called god can compare with our God.

God is the one who truly works wonders, not false gods. He has shown his power openly, so that even other nations saw it. What he did for his people is a lasting sign of his great strength. That gives fresh reason to trust him now.

This points to God bringing Israel out of slavery in Egypt. To "redeem" means to buy back or set free. That rescue was a picture of the greater rescue God would bring through Jesus Christ. Joseph is named alongside Jacob because Joseph's two sons became tribes of Israel, and because Joseph firmly believed God would one day bring his people out.

Now the psalm pictures the crossing of the Red Sea. The waters are described as if they could see God and were afraid. They twisted like a woman in labour and pulled back to make a path. Even the deepest parts of the sea shook before him.

A huge storm breaks out: rain, thunder, lightning flashing like God's arrows, and the earth shaking. Exodus does not mention a storm at the Red Sea. But the ancient Jewish historian Josephus says there was one, and some think these lines also recall the thunder and quaking at Mount Sinai. Either way, all of nature served God as he rescued his people and judged their enemies.

God made a road right through the sea. Then the waters came back, and no footprints were left behind. In the same way, God's ways are often too deep for us to trace. We cannot always explain what he is doing, but we can always trust him.

After the storm comes a gentle picture. God led his people like a shepherd leads his sheep, going ahead of them rather than driving them. He did it through ordinary human leaders, Moses and Aaron. The psalm ends suddenly here, as if remembering God's care was enough to lift the writer's sorrow.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Because the psalm stops so abruptly, some scholars think part of it was lost or that it was never finished. Others reply that the Asaph psalms often end on a scene from history like this one.
